name: The World of AI: AI Courses catalogue page
title: The World of AI: AI Courses catalogue page
answer: This is a catalogue page from The World of AI listing AI courses, with levels, audiences, costs and verification dates. Its most useful point is that the tracked courses split between university graduate courses with public materials and industry courses described as code-first or hands-on, so the choice is about learning style rather than which source is more rigorous. It also states that all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, though the page header says thirteen courses and eleven free.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this catalogue page as part of its AI Research and Learning section. It is a directory of AI courses, described as curated by level and audience with one verified source each. The page states it was last verified on 2026-09-28 and that source links are re-verified daily. It lists course providers, levels, intended audiences and costs, and it says membership is editorial, based on significance rather than sponsorship. The page also notes that skills taught map to the AI Skills Graph. It is a reference catalogue rather than a full course review.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page presents a catalogue of AI courses. Its header says there are 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with companion code, curated by level and audience with a verified source each, and re-verified daily. The body then says all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, and later refers to these ten, so the page contains an internal count discrepancy. It lists providers including DeepLearning.AI on Coursera, Dataquest, fast.ai, DeepLearning.AI with Stanford on Coursera, and university graduate courses from Stanford, UC Berkeley and MIT. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191. The rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. Costs vary: free to audit with a certificate fee, paid certificate, subscription, or free. Only three courses list an accompanying public code repository, fast.ai, Karpathy's Zero to Hero, and MIT's 6.S191. The page says the split matters because university courses are generally structured around exam-driven theory while industry courses are described as code-first or hands-on, so the choice is about how someone wants to learn rather than which source is more rigorous. It also states the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which of these ten is most widely taken.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The page header states 13 AI courses, 11 free, 3 with companion code, re-verified daily. The body states all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, four are university graduate courses, and only three list public code. It gives verification dates of 2026-09-27 for individual courses and 2026-09-28 for the page. It says membership is editorial, not paid placement. It says the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or the most widely taken course. The page also lists site database contents including state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, a glossary, a tools directory, AI companies, a research library, an MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators, and weekly digests.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in Education, this source is useful as a current catalogue of courses and credentials the field uses, with levels, audiences, costs and verification dates. It helps compare university graduate courses against industry courses and shows which include public code. It also flags that the page does not measure enrollment or completion, so it cannot show which courses are most taken or most effective. It is a starting point for finding training options, not an evaluation of learning outcomes.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Education

sections.body: The page is a catalogue, not a review or study. It does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, learner outcomes, or which course is most widely taken. It contains an internal count discrepancy between the header's 13 courses and the body's ten. It is dated by its last verified date of 2026-09-28 and says links are re-verified daily, but the course details may change. It is published by The World of AI and says membership is editorial, not sponsorship, though the page also carries commercial material for books and consulting services by Stephen R. Jordan and SRJ Consulting. It does not provide full syllabi or independent quality assessments.
